title: How does `ServiceLoader` (the Java SPI mechanism) discover implementations (`META-INF/services` files, lazy loading via the context classloader)?
shortTitle: How does ServiceLoader (the Java SPI mechanism) discover implementations?
keyPoints: ServiceLoader discovers implementations of an interface at runtime without the consumer naming concrete classes directly.
On the classpath, providers advertise themselves via a text file at META-INF/services/fully.qualified.InterfaceName listing implementation class names.
In the module system, providers declare `provides ... with` in module-info.java; the compiler verifies the declaration.
Loading is lazy: providers are instantiated only as you iterate, allowing you to stop early or handle per-provider failures.
Discovery uses the thread's context class loader by default, which is the back-channel frameworks use to reach application-level providers.
Service loading is unordered; if you need priority, add your own ranking mechanism.

s1_definition.oneliner: ServiceLoader discovers implementations of an interface by reading META-INF/services files or module provides directives, and lazily instantiates them, decoupling consumers from concrete providers.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Service Provider Interface (SPI)** – a pattern separating the service interface, the provider implementation, and the consumer that needs the capability.
- **`META-INF/services`** – classpath text files listing provider class names; each line is a fully-qualified implementation class.
- **`provides ... with`** – module-system declaration replacing text files; compiler-verified.
- **Lazy loading** – providers are instantiated only as you iterate `ServiceLoader`, not all at once.
- **Context class loader** – the default loader for discovery; lets frameworks reach application-level providers that parent delegation would miss.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants fee calculators from different vendors without hard-coding any vendor's name. The bank publishes a job description (the interface). Vendors drop a signed card into a well-known mailbox (the META-INF services file) saying "my class fulfills that job." When the bank needs calculators, it opens the mailbox, reads every card, and hires each vendor only when actually needed.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ServiceLoader Discovery:

  Provider JARs on classpath:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ gst-fee.jar                                  │
  │ META-INF/services/com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator │
  │   → com.vendor.gst.GstFeeCalculator          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ flat-fee.jar                                 │
  │ META-INF/services/com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator │
  │   → com.vendor.flat.FlatFeeCalculator        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Consumer:
  ServiceLoader.load(FeeCalculator.class)
       │
       ▼ (lazy iteration)
  GstFeeCalculator   → instantiated on first next()
  FlatFeeCalculator  → instantiated on second next()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`ServiceLoader` is Java's built-in SPI mechanism for discovering implementations of an interface at runtime without the consumer naming concrete classes. On the classpath, providers advertise themselves with a text file at `META-INF/services/` listing their class names. In the module system, the `provides ... with` directive in `module-info.java` replaces the text file and is compiler-verified.

The consumer calls `ServiceLoader.load(FeeCalculator.class)` and iterates. Loading is lazy: providers are instantiated only as you iterate, which lets you stop early and handle per-provider failures. Discovery uses the thread's context class loader by default, which is the back-channel frameworks use to reach application-level providers.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj built a billing engine that discovered fee calculators from multiple vendors without editing the engine code. A GST calculator and a flat-fee calculator each shipped their own jar with a `META-INF/services` file. When the engine loaded, `ServiceLoader` found both, applied each to Rajesh's transfer, and summed the fees. Months later, a new vendor added a calculator just by dropping a jar on the classpath.

The senior points are that service loading is unordered, so add your own ranking if you need priority. Iterating can throw `ServiceConfigurationError` for broken providers, so iterate defensively. The payoff is genuine extensibility: add a capability by dropping a jar, with zero changes to the consumer.

Remember one sentence: `ServiceLoader` discovers and lazily loads provider implementations from `META-INF/services` files or module `provides` directives, decoupling the consumer from the concrete provider.
